title: She's Deaf, She's Mute, and She's Bollywood's First Desi Hitwoman
excerpt: Huma Qureshi goes full underworld in 'Baby Do Die Do,' the dark, wild indie dropping alongside Alpha on July 3 — and she doesn't need a spy universe to make you flinch.
body:
July 3 belongs to **Alia Bhatt**. Everyone knows that. *Alpha* has the YRF machine behind it, the spy universe pedigree, and the kind of advance booking numbers that make multiplexes smile. But somewhere in the margins of the same release calendar — deliberately, defiantly — **Huma Qureshi** has placed a bet of her own.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=2rQCZKoaEhc</youtube>

**Baby Do Die Do** is not a franchise. It doesn't have a cinematic universe or a billion-dollar studio backing it. What it has is a premise that lands like a cold slap: a deaf and mute woman who works as a contract killer in Mumbai's underworld, and the only voice she can hear — ever — belongs to her dead sister.

Meet **Baby KarMarKar**, the most unhinged character Bollywood has introduced all year.

Directed by **Nachiket Samant** and produced by Qureshi herself alongside brother **Saqib Saleem** under their **Saleem Siblings** banner, *Baby Do Die Do* is billed as India's first film centred on a desi hitwoman. Baby KarMarKar — a name that sounds like a nursery rhyme and kills like a switchblade — is a woman who cannot speak, cannot hear, and communicates entirely through physicality. No dialogue, no whispered threats, no dramatic monologues. Just a body moving through danger, guided by one spectral voice that shouldn't exist.

It's the kind of role that either makes or breaks a career, and Qureshi has been quietly building toward it for years. From *Gangs of Wasseypur* to *Monica, O My Darling* to her turn as the formidable Taraka in Zack Snyder's *Army of the Dead*, she's always been drawn to women who refuse to sit in the corner. Baby KarMarKar is the logical extreme — a woman so dangerous that the silence around her isn't a disability. It's a weapon.

The supporting cast adds serious texture. **Sikandar Kher** brings his slow-burn menace. **Chunky Panday** shows up with the kind of unhinged energy that tells you this film isn't afraid to get weird. **Seema Pahwa** — national treasure, forever underrated — grounds the whole thing in something real. **Vidya Malvade**, **Arun Kushwah**, and **Himanshu Malik** round out an ensemble that knows how to squeeze every rupee of a tight budget into something that looks five times its cost.

But the film's most unexpected weapon isn't on screen — it's on the dance floor.

**Ishq Kameena 2.0**, the recreated version of the iconic Bollywood track, has quietly become the party anthem of the season. Choreographed by **Remo D'Souza**, the song has taken over club circuits from Mumbai to Ahmedabad. Huma and Saqib have been doing DJ nights across both cities, and the videos coming out show packed dance floors losing their minds to the beat. For a mid-budget film without a studio name attached, that kind of organic musical buzz is absolute gold.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DaNj3AdsFZ-/


> "It strikes the right balance between nostalgia and freshness, appealing both to audiences who grew up with the original and younger listeners discovering the iconic track for the first time." — IWMBuzz

The film begins paid previews tonight — Wednesday, July 2 — with evening shows from 7 PM onwards in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, and Pune, following the new Bollywood trend set by *Dhurandhar The Revenge*, *Bhooth Bangla*, and *Welcome To The Jungle* this year. Full theatrical release follows on Thursday, July 3.

**For NRI audiences**, *Baby Do Die Do* is the kind of film that flies under the radar until someone brings it up at a dinner party. It won't command the massive international screen count of *Alpha*. But if you loved *Gangs of Wasseypur* for its grime, *Ludo* for its beautiful chaos, and *Monica, O My Darling* for its razor-edged wit, this is your film. It's gritty, it's funny, it's a little bit mean — and Huma Qureshi has never looked more committed to owning a screen.

Two badass women are hitting Indian screens on the same day. One commands a spy universe. The other has a dead sister's voice and a loaded gun. It's a very good week to be at the movies.
